newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU unveils farm reform plans for expansion east.
newsitem.headline: EU unveils farm reform plans for expansion east.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday unveiled proposals for further price-cutting farm reforms to prepare for expansion eastwards and prevent the return of costly food mountains.

The proposals, known as Agenda 2000, reinforce 1992 reforms to make European farmers more competitive by lowering prices towards world levels and shifting support for agriculture to direct payments to farmers.
''The time has come to deepen the reform and to take further the movement towards world market prices coupled to direct income aids,'' the European Union executive said in a statement.
It said that the risk of new farm surpluses, another round of world farm trade negotiations starting in 1999, the desire to protect the environment and EU enlargement meant that changes were needed.
A compulsory scheme to cut output by setting aside farmland, unpopular with both farmers and taxpayers, would be suspended if the reform proposals are approved by EU farm ministers.

But in a controversial new move reflecting criticism that cereal farmers have been heavily over-paid, the EU executive proposed that they should only be compensated for half of a planned 20 percent cut in support prices in 2000.
''This payment will be reduced if market prices are sustained at higher levels than currently foreseen,'' it added.

The Commission has estimated that cereals farmers received 8.5 billion European currency units ($9.4 billion) too much over the past four years after a series of crop failures sent world market prices soaring and cuts in EU support prices failed to bite.
The main beneficiaries were wealthy grain barons'' in northern France and Germany and eastern England. About 80 percent of EU farm subsidies are pocketed by 20 percent of the farmers.

The Commission now proposes limiting direct aid payments to individual farmers. While excluding renationalisation, the EU would allow member states to fix criteria for distributing the aid according to commonly agreed rules.
But beef and dairy producers, who face price cuts of 30 percent and 10 percent, respectively, would be more generously compensated than their cereal counterparts.
Overall the compensation payments would add 4.0 billion ecus, or roughly 10 percent, to the EU farm bill.

The eventual entry of 10 eastern European countries, with Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Slovenia in the first wave from 2002 along with Cyprus, would increase EU farmland by half and double the number of farm workers.
Severe income disparities and social distortions would occur in rural areas if the new members received the relatively high EU direct cash payments, the Commission said.
Surpluses would increase after 2001, especially for cereals, sugar, meat and milk, as curbs on subsidised world farm trade begin to bite.
Public stocks of surplus grain are seen surging to 58 million tonnes by 2005, from only two million in 1997. ($ = 0.908 European Currency Unit ECUs)
